Los Angeles, Calif.
In the Interim Report we briefly recounted the background of the present treatment accorded to the Los Angeles area in our regulation of commercial zones and terminal areas, Commercial Zones, 124 M.C.C. at 179-80. We noted that in Los Angeles, Calif., Commercial Zone, 3 M.C.C. 248 (1937), it was determined that the area encompassed by the Los Angeles Harbor districts and Long Beach should be excluded from the Los Angeles commercial zone. This area (San Pedro, Terminal Island, and Wilmington) is connected to the main part of Los Angeles by a narrow strip of annexed land, which is between one-half and three-quarters of a mile wide and known as the "shoestring" strip. An east-west line was defined according to specified streets and city limits and divided the Los Angeles Harbor zone and the Los Angeles commercial zone. Accordingly, freight movements in interstate commerce cannot cross this line without authority from this Commission. The Los Angeles zone and the Los Angeles Harbor zone have each been specifically described according to specified streets and city boundaries.
The division between the harbor area and the main part of Los Angeles was based primarily on a finding that the port was separate from the main residential, business, and industrial sections of Los Angeles. This was evidenced by the fact that in 1937 the two areas were not connected by a major transportation artery or thoroughfare.
